Because CRA tax payments follow specialized federal remittance rules, businesses must verify which payment channels require electronic processing and which still permit physical vouchers.

Corporate Tax, CPP, and RRSP Rules for Salary vs Dividends

Canadian business owners weigh corporate tax deductions, Canada Pension Plan (CPP) remittances, and personal retirement room when deciding between salary and dividends. Business year-end reviews give owners a structured window to compare these direct costs before finalizing annual T4 or T5 slips. Because Alberta does not levy a provincial employer health tax, corporate payroll planning in the province centers primarily on income tax brackets and mandatory CPP contributions.

How T4 Salary Affects Corporate Taxes and Retirement

Paying a T4 salary creates an immediate corporate tax deduction and builds personal retirement capacity through several mechanisms:

  • Corporate Tax Reduction: Wages count as an allowable business expense, lowering net corporate profit and helping active businesses stay below the $500,000 federal small business deduction threshold.
  • RRSP Contribution Room: T4 employment income counts as earned income for tax purposes, generating Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) room equal to 18% of prior-year wages up to the annual federal limit.
  • Mandatory CPP Remittances: Owner-managers paying a salary must remit both the employee and employer portions of CPP, which reduces immediate corporate cash flow but secures an inflation-indexed government pension and disability coverage.
  • Personal Borrowing Verification: Banks and residential mortgage lenders favor recurring T4 pay stubs and T4 slips because they demonstrate steady, predictable employment income.

How T5 Dividends Impact Cash Flow and Lending

Distributing T5 dividends shifts the tax and cash flow profile by drawing directly from after-tax corporate retained earnings:

  • Zero CPP Obligations: Shareholder dividends are exempt from CPP premiums, keeping both the employer and employee contribution amounts inside the company for daily operations or running a growing business.
  • Dividend Gross-Up and Tax Credits: Dividends do not reduce corporate taxable income, but personal tax returns apply a federal and provincial dividend tax credit to account for taxes already paid by the corporation.
  • No New RRSP Room: Because dividends are investment returns rather than earned employment income, they do not generate RRSP contribution room, requiring owners to build retirement savings inside their corporate investment accounts instead.
  • Stricter Underwriting for Loans: Financial institutions often treat dividend payouts as variable distributions and request two to three years of corporate financial statements before approving personal mortgages.

Long-term wealth transfer planning depends heavily on how much retained earnings remain inside the corporation versus how much cash moves into personal hands each year.

Combined corporate and personal tax rates under Canadian tax integration typically bring the net after-tax difference between salary and dividends within 1% to 2%. Consequently, business life cycle stage, personal financing goals, and corporate cash flow requirements dictate how owners get paid rather than tax rates alone. Shareholders who plan for wealth transfer or operational expansion must balance immediate household income against capital retained inside the company.

Establishing a Baseline T4 Salary

Paying yourself a scheduled T4 salary builds the verifiable earned income history that Canadian banks and mortgage underwriters demand for personal financing. Regular payroll remittances also generate Registered Retirement Savings Plan (RRSP) contribution room (18% of prior-year earned income up to the annual Canada Revenue Agency limit) and qualify working parents to deduct child care expenses on their T1 personal tax returns.

Distributing Surplus Profits as T5 Dividends

After your corporation covers operating overhead, tax installments, and base payroll, directors can declare eligible or non-eligible dividends from retained earnings. T5 distributions let shareholders withdraw excess cash on demand without triggering mandatory Canada Pension Plan (CPP) source deductions. Where family members actively work in the business or meet Tax on Split Income (TOSI) exclusions, dividend declarations can also distribute income across adult shareholders.

How Canadian Tax Integration Prevents Corporate Double Taxation

Canadian tax integration keeps the combined corporate and personal tax burden within a 1% to 2% variance whether an owner-manager takes a T4 salary or a T5 dividend. Because the Canada Revenue Agency equalizes total tax outcomes across both payout methods, business owners should never select a compensation structure solely to avoid perceived double taxation.

Gross-Up and Dividend Tax Credit Mechanics

Shareholders receive dividends out of after-tax corporate retained earnings, which creates a common misconception that the same dollar faces full taxation twice. Rather than taxing corporate profits a second time at full personal rates, the federal and provincial tax systems apply a two-step adjustment on your T1 return:

  • Dividend Gross-Up: Your personal tax calculation inflates the actual dividend received to approximate the pre-tax profit the corporation earned before paying corporate income tax.
  • Dividend Tax Credit: Coordinate your personal tax returns with your corporate filings to claim this direct tax credit, which offsets the corporate tax already remitted at year-end.

While the gross-up and tax credit neutralize double taxation, T5 dividends do not count as earned income for federal tax purposes. Paying yourself a T4 salary generates new RRSP contribution room equal to 18% of your prior year's earned income up to the annual CRA ceiling, and unlocks personal tax deductions for childcare expenses. KWB CPAs frequently advise shareholders that chasing slightly lower immediate personal tax rates on dividends can cost decades of tax-sheltered retirement compounding.

Hidden Cash Flow Traps of 100% Dividend Payouts

Relying exclusively on T5 dividends eliminates monthly payroll remittances, but that administrative convenience creates personal cash flow and financing hurdles. Unlike T4 payroll, which deducts income tax at source on every paycheque, dividends arrive in your personal bank account with zero tax withheld. Owners who do not manually segregate personal tax reserves often face steep out-of-pocket balances in April alongside mandatory quarterly tax installments.

Pulling all after-tax corporate surplus into personal accounts also strips the company of working capital needed for equipment upgrades or seasonal slowdowns. Building a corporate wealth management plan alongside a steady base T4 wage gives mortgage lenders verifiable employment income while automating baseline personal tax remittances.

Navigating the intricacies of compensation for Canadian business owners, particularly the choice between dividend vs salary, often leads to specific questions. This section addresses common inquiries to help clarify these important financial decisions.

QuestionAnswer
Which compensation option offers better long-term savings opportunities like CPP and RRSP contributions?A salary contributes directly to your Canada Pension Plan (CPP) and allows for registered retirement savings plan (RRSP) contributions based on earned income. Dividends, however, do not generate CPP contributions and do not create RRSP room. If building a strong retirement fund through these avenues is a priority, a salary may be more beneficial.

Discussing your family's situation with an accountant at KWB Accountants & Advisors can clarify the best approach for your specific circumstances.

Should a Canadian business owner consider a combination of both salary and dividends?Yes, many Canadian business owners use a hybrid approach, taking a modest salary for CPP and some earned income, then supplementing with dividends as corporate profits allow. This strategy can balance tax efficiency with personal financial goals, such as building retirement savings and having some predictable income. How Short-Term Disability Plans Lower Employer EI Costs

Canadian employers pay 1.4 times the employee contribution rate for Employment Insurance (EI) on every dollar of insurable earnings up to the annual federal ceiling. When you improve your profit by registering a qualified wage-loss replacement plan with Service Canada, you reduce that 1.4x multiplier and keep more capital inside your business.

Federal EI rules cover more than involuntary job loss. Workers also claim special benefits during medical leave, non-workplace injuries, or parental leave. Providing a workplace short-term disability plan gives staff immediate income replacement during illness or injury, which eliminates or shortens their reliance on government EI sickness benefits.

  • Lower Payroll Tax Rates: Service Canada grants approved employers a reduced EI premium multiplier below the standard 1.4x rate because company-funded plans lower claims against the public EI fund.
  • Stronger Employee Retention: Companies running a growing business attract and keep skilled talent by offering reliable wage protection alongside statutory benefits.
  • Shared Financial Return: Federal regulations require employers to return 5/12ths of the premium savings to the employees covered by the plan, either through cash rebates or expanded workplace benefits., while the business retains 7/12ths directly on the bottom line.

Why Estate Planning and Accounting Belong Together

Wealth rarely moves in a straight line from one generation to the next. Along the way there are taxes, corporate structures, family dynamics, and paperwork that has to match what the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) expects. Estate planning is often treated as a legal exercise: wills, trusts, and powers of attorney. Accounting is treated as something you deal with every year at tax time. In practice, the two are the same project viewed from different angles. If the books, ownership records, and tax history are not clear while you are building the plan, the transition can cost more in tax, delay, and stress than it needs to.

What a Smooth Transition Actually Requires

A smooth handoff of wealth is not only about who receives what. It is about whether the next owner can operate without surprises. That usually means you have up-to-date financial statements for operating companies and holding companies, a clear list of assets, liabilities, and related-party balances, documentation for shares, partnership interests, and major contracts, personal and corporate tax filings that align with how the business is actually run, and a realistic picture of tax that may be triggered on death, on a sale, or on a reorganization. When those pieces are missing, families often discover problems at the worst time: during an illness, after a sudden death, or in the middle of a sale.

How the GST Quick Method Works and Who Qualifies

Canadian small businesses with annual gross revenues under $400,000, including GST, can elect to use the GST Quick Method to simplify tax filings and reduce their annual remittance. Eligibility and Remittance Rates

The $400,000 gross revenue threshold (doubled from the pre-2013 limit of $200,000) combines both taxable sales and the 5% GST billed on client invoices. Under the standard filing approach, registrants track every dollar of GST collected and subtract eligible Input Tax Credits (ITCs) paid on daily operating expenses. Under the Quick Method, businesses charge customers the standard 5% GST rate but remit a lower fixed percentage of gross GST-included revenue to the CRA.):

  • Capital asset ITC exception: Registrants waive ITCs on routine operating overhead in exchange for reduced remittance rates but can still claim full ITCs on capital property purchases like commercial vehicles or major equipment.
  • Eligible business types: Most service-based companies and qualifying retailers or resellers of goods can elect into this calculation method.
